Questions.QuestionText: If P(A) = 0.5 and P(B|A) = 0.4, what is P(A ∩ B)?

Questions.Title: Question 479
Questions.QuestionText: Two events with non-zero probabilities can be:
Questions.Feedback: Events with non-zero probabilities can be independent but not mutually exclusive. If they were mutually exclusive, P(A ∩ B) = 0, which contradicts the independence criterion P(A ∩ B) = P(A)×P(B) ≠ 0

Questions.Title: Question 480
Questions.QuestionText: If you flip a fair coin 4 times, what is the probability of getting at least one head?
Questions.Feedback: P(at least one head) = 1 - P(no heads) = 1 - P(all tails) = 1 - (1/2)^4 = 1 - 1/16 = 15/16 = 0.9375

Questions.Title: Question 481
Questions.QuestionText: If P(A|C) = P(A) and P(B|C) = P(B), then events A and B are:
Questions.Feedback: This is the definition of conditional independence given C, meaning that when C occurs, knowing about A doesn't change the probability of B and vice versa

Questions.Title: Question 482
Questions.QuestionText: In a Venn diagram of events A and B, the region where A and B overlap represents:
Questions.Feedback: The overlap region in a Venn diagram represents the intersection of the two events - outcomes that belong to both event A and event B, denoted P(A ∩ B)

Questions.Title: Question 483
Questions.QuestionText: Which statement is true about disjoint (mutually exclusive) events A and B?
Questions.Feedback: For mutually exclusive events, P(A ∩ B) = 0, so P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = 0/P(B) = 0, assuming P(B) > 0

Questions.Title: Question 484
Questions.QuestionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the basic axioms of probability?
Questions.Feedback: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) is only true for mutually exclusive events. The general formula is P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B)

Options.Text: P(Ω) = 1, where Ω is the sample space
For any two events A and B, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)
If A₁, A₂, ... are mutually exclusive events, then P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ ...) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) + ...

Questions.Title: Question 485
Questions.QuestionText: What is the sample space for the experiment of rolling two fair dice and recording the sum?
Questions.Feedback: When rolling two dice and recording their sum, the possible outcomes are the integers from 2 to 12 inclusive

Questions.Title: Question 486
Questions.QuestionText: A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. If the first ball drawn is red, what is the probability the second is also red?
Questions.Feedback: After drawing a red ball, 3 red and 6 blue balls remain. The probability of drawing another red is 3/(3+6) = 3/9 = 1/3

Questions.Title: Question 487
Questions.QuestionText: Given P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.12, are events A and B independent?
Questions.Feedback: Events A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Here, P(A) × P(B) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12 = P(A ∩ B), so they are independent

Questions.Title: Question 488
Questions.QuestionText: From a standard 52-card deck, you draw 2 cards without replacement. What is the probability of drawing 2 aces?
Questions.Feedback: The probability of the first card being an ace is 4/52. After drawing an ace, there are 3 aces left among 51 cards, so the probability of the second card being an ace is 3/51. Therefore, P(2 aces) = (4/52) × (3/51) = 1/221

Questions.Title: Question 489
Questions.QuestionText: When rolling a fair six-sided die once, which is NOT an event?
Questions.Feedback: An event must be a subset of the sample space. Since the sample space for a six-sided die is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, getting a 7 is not a possible outcome and thus not an event

Questions.Title: Question 490
Questions.QuestionText: In how many ways can you select 3 cards from a standard 52-card deck?
Questions.Feedback: The number of ways to select 3 cards from 52 cards is C(52,3) = 52! / (3! × 49!) = 22,100

Questions.Title: Question 491
Questions.QuestionText: Which formula correctly defines P(A|B)?
Questions.Feedback: The conditional probability of A given B is defined as P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), where P(B) > 0

Questions.Title: Question 492
Questions.QuestionText: For any event A, which formula is always true?
Questions.Feedback: For any event A, P(A) + P(A') = 1, since an event either occurs or it doesn't, and these are mutually exclusive and exhaustive possibilities

Questions.Title: Question 493
Questions.QuestionText: In a room of 23 people, the probability that at least 2 people share a birthday is approximately:
Questions.Feedback: In the Birthday Problem, with 23 people the probability of at least one shared birthday is approximately 0.507 (slightly greater than 0.5), which is surprisingly high for many people

Questions.Title: Question 494
Questions.QuestionText: Which of the following best describes the Central Limit Theorem?
Questions.Feedback: The Central Limit Theorem states that the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as the sample size increases, regardless of the shape of the population distribution.

Options.Text: The sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as the sample size increases, regardless of the shape of the population distribution.
The sample mean will always equal the population mean regardless of sample size.
The standard deviation of a sample is always smaller than the population standard deviation.
The sampling distribution is always normally distributed regardless of sample size.

Questions.Title: Question 495
Questions.QuestionText: If a population has a standard deviation of 15, what is the standard error of the mean for a sample of size 25?
Questions.Feedback: The standard error of the mean is σ/√n = 15/√25 = 15/5 = 3.

Questions.Title: Question 496
Questions.QuestionText: How does increasing the sample size affect the standard error of the mean?
Questions.Feedback: As the sample size (n) increases, the denominator in the standard error formula (σ/√n) increases, which decreases the standard error.

Options.Text: It has no effect on the standard error.
It can either increase or decrease the standard error, depending on the population.

Questions.Title: Question 497
Questions.QuestionText: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean has a width of 10 units. What would be the approximate width of a 99% confidence interval using the same sample?
Questions.Feedback: The width of a 95% CI is 10 units = 2 × 1.96 × SE. For 99% CI, width ≈ 2 × 2.576 × SE ≈ (2.576/1.96) × 10 ≈ 1.315 × 10 ≈ 13 units.

Questions.Title: Question 498
Questions.QuestionText: To decrease the margin of error in a confidence interval by half, what should be done to the sample size?
Questions.Feedback: Since margin of error ∝ 1/√n, to reduce it by half, we need √n to double. This means n must be quadrupled.

Questions.Title: Question 499
Questions.QuestionText: When sampling from a highly skewed population distribution, approximately what minimum sample size is typically needed for the Central Limit Theorem to ensure the sampling distribution of means is approximately normal?
Questions.Feedback: A commonly cited rule of thumb is that for highly skewed distributions, a sample size of at least 30 is generally required for the sampling distribution to be approximately normal.

Questions.Title: Question 500
Questions.QuestionText: What does the standard error of the mean represent?
Questions.Feedback: The standard error of the mean represents the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean, indicating how much sample means vary from sample to sample.

Options.Text: The standard deviation of the population
The standard deviation of the sample
The expected difference between the sample mean and the true population mean
The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean

Questions.Title: Question 501
Questions.QuestionText: A population has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10. If samples of size 64 are taken, what is the approximate probability that a sample mean will be greater than 52?
Questions.Feedback: Using CLT, the sampling distribution has mean 50 and standard error 10/√64 = 1.25. Standardizing: Z = (52-50)/1.25 = 1.6. P(Z > 1.6) = 0.0668.

Questions.Title: Question 502
Questions.QuestionText: Which of the following is the correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval?
Questions.Feedback: A 95% confidence interval means that if we were to take many samples and compute a 95% confidence interval from each sample, about 95% of those intervals would contain the population mean.

Options.Text: There is a 95% probability that the population mean falls within the interval.
If we were to take many samples and compute a 95% confidence interval from each sample, about 95% of those intervals would contain the population mean.
95% of the sample data falls within the interval.
The sample mean has a 95% chance of being the true population mean.

Questions.Title: Question 503
Questions.QuestionText: A researcher wants to estimate a population mean with a margin of error of no more than 2 units with 95% confidence. The population standard deviation is 8. What minimum sample size is needed?

Questions.Title: Question 504
Questions.QuestionText: How is the standard error of the mean related to the population standard deviation?
Questions.Feedback: The standard error of the mean is calculated as σ/√n, where σ is the population standard deviation and n is the sample size.

Options.Text: Standard error is always larger than the standard deviation
Standard error equals the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size
Standard error equals the standard deviation multiplied by the sample size

Questions.Title: Question 505
Questions.QuestionText: According to the Central Limit Theorem, which of the following is NOT necessary for the sampling distribution of the mean to be approximately normal?
Questions.Feedback: According to the CLT, the sampling distribution of the mean will be approximately normal regardless of the shape of the population distribution, as long as the sample size is sufficiently large.

Options.Text: The sample size must be sufficiently large
The population distribution must be normal
The population must have a finite variance

Questions.Title: Question 506
Questions.QuestionText: A confidence interval for a population mean is given as 45 ± 3. What is the margin of error?
Questions.Feedback: The margin of error is 3, as it represents how far the confidence interval extends in either direction from the point estimate (45).

Questions.Title: Question 507
Questions.QuestionText: What happens to the width of a confidence interval if the confidence level is increased from 95% to 99%, while keeping everything else the same?
Questions.Feedback: As the confidence level increases, the z-critical value increases, which makes the margin of error larger and therefore the confidence interval wider.

Options.Text: The width could either increase or decrease, depending on the sample size

Questions.Title: Question 508
Questions.QuestionText: For which of the following population distributions would the Central Limit Theorem be MOST important when working with sample means?
Questions.Feedback: The Central Limit Theorem is most important for highly skewed distributions like the exponential distribution, as it allows us to use normal-based methods even when the underlying population is far from normal.

Questions.Title: Question 509
Questions.QuestionText: As the sample size increases, what happens to the sampling distribution of the sample mean?
Questions.Feedback: As the sample size increases, the sampling distribution becomes more normal (regardless of the original population distribution) and its variance decreases (since standard error = σ/√n).

Options.Text: Its mean shifts away from the population mean
It becomes more normal and its variance decreases

Questions.Title: Question 510
Questions.QuestionText: A population has a mean of 75 and a standard deviation of 12. If a sample of size 36 has a mean of 72, what is the z-score of this sample mean?

Questions.Title: Question 511
Questions.QuestionText: Which of the following is NOT a component used in calculating a confidence interval for a population mean?
Questions.Feedback: The confidence interval formula uses the sample mean, critical value, and standard error (which is calculated using the sample standard deviation), but not the population variance directly.

Questions.Title: Question 512
Questions.QuestionText: What is the mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean?
Questions.Feedback: The mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean is equal to the population mean, making the sample mean an unbiased estimator of the population mean.

Options.Text: Equal to the population mean minus the standard error
Equal to the population mean divided by the sample size

Questions.Title: Question 513
Questions.QuestionText: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is (42, 50). What is the point estimate of the population mean?
Questions.Feedback: The point estimate is the sample mean, which is at the center of the confidence interval: (42 + 50)/2 = 46.

Questions.Title: Question 514
Questions.QuestionText: To reduce the margin of error by a factor of 3, by what factor should the sample size be increased?
Questions.Feedback: Since margin of error ∝ 1/√n, to reduce it by a factor of 3, we need √n to be 3 times larger. This means n must be 3² = 9 times larger.

Questions.Title: Question 515
Questions.QuestionText: Which of the following is an assumption of the Central Limit Theorem?
Questions.Feedback: The Central Limit Theorem assumes that the samples are random and independent. It does not require the population to be normally distributed or have a specific sample size.

Options.Text: The population must be normally distributed
The sample size must be at least 100
The population mean must be known

Questions.Title: Question 516
Questions.QuestionText: If the population standard deviation is unknown, what is used in its place when calculating the standard error of the mean?
Questions.Feedback: When the population standard deviation is unknown, we use the sample standard deviation as an estimate when calculating the standard error of the mean.

Options.Text: The interquartile range of the sample
The median absolute deviation of the sample

Questions.Title: Question 517
Questions.QuestionText: How do outliers in a sample typically affect the width of a confidence interval for the mean?
Questions.Feedback: Outliers typically increase the sample standard deviation, which increases the standard error and therefore the width of the confidence interval.

Options.Text: They have no effect on the width
They tend to increase the width
They tend to decrease the width
They always make the confidence interval invalid

Questions.Title: Question 518
Questions.QuestionText: A population has a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 20. If samples of size 25 are taken, what is the approximate probability that a sample mean will be between 95 and 105?
Questions.Feedback: Using CLT, the sampling distribution has mean 100 and standard error 20/√25 = 4. The standardized interval is (95-100)/4 to (105-100)/4 = -1.25 to 1.25. P(-1.25 < Z < 1.25) ≈ 0.6826.

Questions.Title: Question 519
Questions.QuestionText: What is the variance of the sampling distribution of the sample mean?
Questions.Feedback: The variance of the sampling distribution of the sample mean is σ²/n, where σ² is the population variance and n is the sample size.

Options.Text: Equal to the population variance divided by the sample size
Equal to the population variance multiplied by the sample size

Questions.Title: Question 520
Questions.QuestionText: Which of the following is an incorrect interpretation of a 95% confidence interval for a population mean?
Questions.Feedback: The incorrect interpretation is that there is a 95% probability the population mean falls within the specific interval. In frequentist statistics, the population mean is fixed (not random), so it either is or isn't in the interval (with 100% or 0% probability).

Options.Text: We are 95% confident that the interval contains the population mean
About 95% of similarly constructed intervals would contain the population mean
There is a 95% probability that the population mean falls within this specific interval
If we repeated the study many times, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the population mean

Questions.Title: Question 521
Questions.QuestionText: If the sample size is quadrupled, what happens to the width of a confidence interval (assuming everything else remains constant)?
Questions.Feedback: The width of a confidence interval is proportional to 1/√n. If n is quadrupled, the width is reduced by a factor of 1/√4 = 1/2.

Options.Text: It increases by a factor of 2
It decreases by a factor of 2
It decreases by a factor of 2
It decreases by a factor of 4

Questions.Title: Question 522
Questions.QuestionText: A researcher wants to estimate a population mean with a margin of error of no more than 5 units with 95% confidence. The population standard deviation is 20. What minimum sample size is needed?

Questions.Title: Question 523
Questions.QuestionText: For which of the following would you need the LARGEST sample size for the Central Limit Theorem to apply well?
Questions.Feedback: A highly right-skewed distribution with outliers deviates most strongly from normality, requiring the largest sample size for the sampling distribution to be approximately normal.

Options.Text: A highly right-skewed distribution with outliers

Questions.Title: Question 524
Questions.QuestionText: What is the critical value for a 90% confidence interval of a population mean?
Questions.Feedback: For a 90% confidence interval, we need the z-score with 5% in each tail, so z = 1.645.

Questions.Title: Question 525
Questions.QuestionText: A sample of 64 observations has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 8. What is the width of a 95% confidence interval for the population mean?
Questions.Feedback: The margin of error is 1.96*8/√64 = 1.96*8/8 = 1.96, so the width is 2*1.96 = 3.92.

Questions.Title: Question 526
Questions.QuestionText: A researcher wants to estimate a population proportion with a margin of error of no more than 0.04 with 95% confidence. No prior information about the proportion is available. What minimum sample size is needed?
Questions.Feedback: With no prior information, we use p = 0.5 for maximum variance: n = (1.96²*0.5*0.5)/0.04² = 0.9604/0.0016 = 600.25, rounded up to 601.

Questions.Title: Question 527
Questions.QuestionText: In which situation would the sampling distribution of a sample proportion NOT be approximately normal?
Questions.Feedback: For the sample size of 20 and proportion of 0.05, np = 20*0.05 = 1, which is less than 10, so the normal approximation would not work well.

Options.Text: The sample size is 50 and the population proportion is 0.5
The sample size is 100 and the population proportion is 0.3
The sample size is 20 and the population proportion is 0.05
The sample size is 200 and the population proportion is 0.1

Questions.Title: Question 528
Questions.QuestionText: If the standard error of the mean for a sample of size 25 is 2, what would be the standard error for a sample of size 100 from the same population?
Questions.Feedback: If SE₁ = σ/√n₁ = 2 for n₁ = 25, then SE₂ = σ/√n₂ = σ/√100 = σ/10. Since σ = 2*√25 = 2*5 = 10, SE₂ = 10/10 = 1.
